newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Wary of China, Taiwan touts Okinawa investments.
newsitem.headline: Wary of China, Taiwan touts Okinawa investments.

text.p: Taiwan's ruling Nationalist Party said on Thursday it would organise a business mission to Okinawa in November, hoping to nudge Taiwan investors toward Japan's southernmost island -- and away from arch rival China.

Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui expressed his "full support" for the scheme after being briefed on Wednesday by Liu Tai-ying, head of the Nationalist Party's business management committee, spokesman Lin Shou-che told Reuters by telephone.
Lee is also chairman of the Nationalist Party, one of the world's richest political organisations with T$37.8 billion (US$1.4 billion) in assets under seven holding companies.
Lee and other party leaders, wary of a risky overdependence on the economy of Taiwan's longtime adversary, have called for diverting investment away from the communist mainland.
"The plan is aimed at leading local companies to diversify investment to Okinawa, so as to prevent them from too much concentration on mainland China," spokesman Lin said.

The new ruling party strategy is to stress investment in areas within three time zones and having convenient transport links to Taiwan, which China has regarded as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949.

Okinawa, one of Japan's poorer prefectures, is as near to Taiwan as China and has direct air and sea links. Taiwan has banned direct transport, communications and other official links with China for nearly five decades.
"Chairman Liu said Okinawa's tourism, electronics processing and aerospace industries are all investment-worthy," Lin said.

Taiwan-Japan ties have been strained recently by a popular backlash against Japanese assertions of sovereignty over a chain of East China Sea islands, known as the Diaoyus in China and the Senkakus in Japan. The islands also are claimed by Taipei and Beijing.

Analysts said the Okinawa scheme was likely to be attacked by the opposition New Party and conservative Nationalists who suspect that President Lee, who was educated in Japan and speaks Japanese, is politically too close to Tokyo.
Tokyo has diplomatic ties only with Beijing, but has close economic and cultural ties with Taiwan dating to a half century of colonial rule that ended with Japan's World War Two defeat.
In recent years, party-owned businesses have boosted investment in Southeast Asia in response to the government's "southbound policy" -- an earlier scheme to divert investors away from China.
Companies controlled by the Nationalists' holding companies generated pretax profits of five billion Taiwanese dollars (US$182 million) in the first half of 1996 alone, Lin said.
